"People swimming in the pool" (2022) is one of the works by Vicente Siso that will be exhibited at the Tierra del Sol gallery starting on January 13 (photo courtesy of Vicente Siso)

Tierra del Sol is pleased to present "Vicente Siso: Memories of Land and Water" at the gallery's new location in West Hollywood. Siso is an artist from the Studio Arts Program since 2012, and this exhibition marks his debut as a solo artist. Born in Madrid in 1962, he grew up alternating between Venezuela, Trinidad, and Miami. At around 20 years old, he moved with his family to Southern California.

Working with expertise in various themes, Siso has created a prolific series of landscapes, portraits, and still lifes in acrylic, pastel, pencil, and watercolor. Drawing from family portraits, his own photographs, and his memories, his colorful compositions demonstrate a wide range of interests and skill with different media. Siso's tropical and marine landscapes reflect the geographies of his past, using rich patterns and incorporating people to create meaningful connections between culture, memory, and the environment. Siso titles his works in a mix of Spanish and English, highlighting the complex nature of his life in Los Angeles County. "Vicente Siso: Memories of Land and Water" opens to the public on Saturday, January 13th, with a reception from 6 to 8 p.m. The exhibition will remain open until Sunday, March 3rd.
The Tierra del Sol gallery is located at 7414 Santa Monica Blvd. For more information, please visit tierradelsolgallery.org.
Adapt existing methods and incorporate new approaches to solve the problem.

At the district level, we can look at the Sydney business district as an example of an area that developed its pre-colonial landscape into a city with two distinct heights – initially with a maximum height of 45 meters, and then with the towering skyscrapers of today. On a much smaller scale, the same thing can happen in the urban centers of Sydney located around transportation hubs. Suburban areas also need to evolve, with a trend towards more affordable housing with heights below the treetops in key locations. Obviously, new residential development must be well-designed and include trees, parks, and gardens, as well as other essential infrastructure.

Our planning system also needs to adapt so that planners in suburban municipalities (who seem less open to change) are not the only ones determining the future shape of their suburban areas. One way to move forward could be to establish an independent decision-making body that advocates for high-quality designs, provided they remain below the height of the trees, include family homes, large balconies, and community gardens, and also have an aesthetically pleasing appearance. This could be the role of the current architect for the New South Wales government, working within the framework of a carefully crafted code of compliance.

Over the past decade, our lives have changed thanks to technology. Many people now work from home, and Sydney boasts an impressive network of subways and light rail. The ability to shop online has also changed the way we shop, and friends and family seem to be closer thanks to smartphone communication. These types of transitions from one system to another can also occur in existing buildings in our area, through a planning approach focused on adaptive reuse rather than prioritizing the preservation of heritage.

Chris Johnson was a former architect for the New South Wales government (1995-2005) and the chief executive of the New South Wales Department of Planning (2005-2009). He served as the chief executive of Urban Taskforce Australia from 2011 to 2019.
One final push for gender equality
Last year, the World Economic Forum predicted that it would take five generations to achieve gender equality in all nations. Now, the World Bank wants to speed up that timeline.

The international financial institution is prepared to launch a strategy aimed at significantly promoting the economic rights and opportunities for girls and women by 2030. The plan focuses on improving inclusion and resilience through access to financing, technological innovation, and changes in legislation and public policies.

“Recent research shows that both social norms and attitudes can change; for example, that involving men and boys can foster their support and acceptance of gender equality,” states a draft of the plan. “Positive outcomes in terms of gender equality can be accelerated and expanded through a better understanding of […] how social norms and attitudes determine daily expectations, priorities, and practices.”

Changes in mindset are more difficult to quantify than loans to rural women, or the education of girls. However, there is ample evidence that women's action can move mountains. For example, in Iran, women have posed the greatest threat to the Islamic government in 40 years simply by refusing to comply with laws that require them to cover their hair. In some of the 130 countries with minimum quotas for female representation in government, such as India, resistance from men to female voting and political activism has decreased.

In some rural communities in Africa, civil society organizations are replacing a harmful initiation ritual with health education. One such program helped Kamanda Timayio, the leader of the Maasai village of Maparasha (Kenya), to change his views on female genital mutilation. He told Le Monde that he had "left behind ignorance" and that he would abandon the practice.

The World Bank cites other examples. From 1970 to 2022, Bangladesh quadrupled female literacy rates and doubled the female participation rate in the active workforce. Its gross domestic product tripled significantly. This change gained momentum on its own. Hiring women as teachers and healthcare workers within their own communities fostered confidence and "made women's mobility and employment more socially acceptable."

The bank's plan focuses on regulations and institutions that may still require generational changes. Rwanda took over two decades to establish itself as a model for agricultural reform that promotes women's economic empowerment: "No one benefits if women are suppressed," said Rwandan President Paul Kagame, defending agricultural reform in 2015. "We need to change the mindset, not just the laws."
The World Bank hopes to spread that message.
German farmers, ranchers, and machinery operators are causing concern for business leaders.

In Germany, where workers and employers jointly manage many companies, a large strike is quite unusual. A wave of large strikes is almost unheard of. Currently, the country of "co-management" is facing, simultaneously, an eight-day "action week" by angry farmers and ranchers who have blocked roads with tractors, a three-day strike by railway workers, and, to top it all off, an imminent strike by doctors, who have already closed their offices during the Christmas and New Year period. This "action week," as it has begun to be called, will put the harmonious German labor relations to the test in the new year.

The protests were largely triggered by the government's decision to end subsidies for agricultural fuel and the tax exemptions for agricultural vehicles. These measures pushed farmers to the brink. They also mobilized other workers, who were already frustrated by the pressure of inflation, the recession, and the austerity measures imposed by the government. On January 9th, Deutsche Bahn employees, the national railway company, began a strike over working hours and wages.

In an effort to ease tensions with farmers and ranchers, the government agreed to a gradual reduction in the fuel subsidy over three years, as well as the maintenance of the exemption from vehicle taxes. However, farmers dismissed these concessions as being insufficient. On January 4th, a group of these farmers prevented Robert Habeck, the Minister of Economy, from disembarking from a ferry upon his return from a family vacation. According to the think tank IW Köln, if train drivers end up being equally unimpressed, the strike could be costly for German companies. The strike could cost companies 100 million euros (110 million US dollars) per day if it leads to a disruption in production. The automotive, chemical, and steel industries, which are the most important in Germany, are particularly reliant on rail transport.

The mood of the workers remains completely unchanged. Habeck warns that "there are calls circulating with revolutionary fantasies." The far-right party, Alternative for Germany, is doing everything it can to fuel the demands. In Dresden, the "Free Saxons," another far-right group, infiltrated the farmers' protest, demanding the "abolition of the traffic light" (referring to the ruling coalition of social democrats, liberals, and Greens, named after their party colors).

Thomas Puls, from IW Köln, fears that strikes will damage Germany's image as a business hub. Local business owners are already concerned about a German version of the 2018 "Yellow Vests" protests in France, which culminated in demonstrators dressed in that manner setting cars on fire on the Champs-Élysées and the police using tear gas. Jochen Kopelke, head of the German police union, warned in an interview with the Tagesspiegel that farmers were "likely just the beginning of a huge wave of protests this year." Germany was the only major economy to contract in 2023, and the year ended on a particularly sour note, with an unexpected drop in business confidence in December. This year looks even more challenging.
Breweries are challenging the exemption of waste regulations for wine producers.

While the EU is debating regulations to reduce packaging waste, brewers argue that they are being unfairly discriminated against due to exemptions for wine producers in the reuse and deposit-return targets and plans. However, one of the leaders of the European wine industry association stated that brewers should "focus on their own issues."

European brewers are warning that exempting wine from deposit, return, and reuse schemes while not doing so for beer is unfair and potentially illegal. Meanwhile, lawmakers are in final negotiations on a new law aimed at significantly reducing packaging waste across the EU.

The environment ministers agreed on a negotiating mandate from the European Council regarding the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) to be finalized before Christmas, paving the way for upcoming political discussions with the European Parliament, which are already underway at the technical level.

The European Brewers' Association responded to MEPs and government negotiators, stating that "our position is clear" (January 10). "If the objectives and legal requirements of the PPWR are applied to beer, then there is a legal obligation to apply them to all categories of alcoholic beverages."

The ministerial summit on December 18th allowed wine producers to avoid the requirement that, by the end of the decade, 10% of their products must be supplied in reusable packaging through a reuse or refill system, increasing this figure to 40% by 2040. This exemption would also apply to the requirement, also supported by the European Parliament, that wine should be exempt from deposit-return schemes that are planned to be implemented in 2029 according to the proposal.

Both the Czech and Belgian ministers immediately expressed their reservations at the December 18 summit regarding the unequal treatment of breweries, but they ultimately accepted the agreement. Belgium, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the EU Council and is therefore, in principle, neutral in the intergovernmental negotiations, hopes to reach an agreement with the parliament by early March.

Ignacio Sánchez Recarte, the general secretary of the wine producers' association, Comité Européen des Entreprises Vins, which represents approximately 7,000 wine producers across Europe, disagrees with the concerns raised by beer manufacturers. He stated to Euronews that a market dominated by large, multinational beer companies cannot be compared to one almost entirely made up of small, national producers.

Sánchez Recarte stated that more than 99% of the national producers in the sector are small or medium-sized businesses, thus questioning the validity of the legal arguments presented by the breweries and reaffirming that their organization has been responsible for providing political decision-makers with "relevant and appropriate" information for their industry.

Sánchez Recarte stated that "It is not my role to determine whether the beer industry should take on this or another objective, as it should depend on the inherent characteristics of its own sector. Similarly, breweries should focus on their own affairs and prioritize their own responsibilities."

European brewers shared a brief legal analysis with Euronews, which was sent to the European Commission last year. The analysis argues that wine and beer are competing products and that they are "at least partially, substitutable," and that regulations favoring one over the other would distort the market.

Simon Spillane, head of operations for the lobbying group, stated that the breweries are "already leading the way" in terms of sustainable packaging, citing the example of beer barrels that are reused approximately 165 times before being crushed and recycled after 30 years. He assures that they support reuse and recycling systems in many countries.

Spillane stated that “Therefore, we advocate for an ambitious PPWR, but we need equal conditions in packaging legislation, where beer and other alcoholic beverages are subject to the same rules, with each sector contributing fairly to achieve the goals and support collection systems. Any other approach puts brewers at a competitive disadvantage.”
The Biden administration allows corporate criminals to get away with their actions.

Tim Whitehouse, a former legal enforcement attorney at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the current CEO of Public Works for Environmental Responsibility, praised the Biden administration for recent improvements in law enforcement, while also acknowledging the strong opposition these efforts generate. "Building an effective law enforcement program requires sustained funding and political support," he told me. "The instability in Congress is not only demoralizing EPA employees, but it also undermines their ability to think strategically in the long term."

The EPA's challenges are distinct, but not unrelated, to those of the Department of Justice, which enforces environmental crimes through its Environmental and Natural Resources Division (ENRD). Prior to joining the EPA, Uhlmann, the EPA's Deputy Secretary for Law Enforcement, had been the head of the ENRD's Criminal Section for many years, from 1990 to 2007. The EPA transfers its most serious civil and criminal cases to the ENRD, which, being a relatively under-funded office, often relies on other agencies to decide which cases to pursue. In the 2022 fiscal year, the EPA referred fewer cases to the Department of Justice (DOJ) (88), which was the lowest number since 2000, and also concluded fewer court cases than it had closed up to that point. As the Environmental Integrity Project notes, even the Trump-era EPA concluded 94 civil cases and referred an average of 106 cases to the DOJ each year.

The Justice Department's broad approach to corporate crime has been the subject of intense scrutiny from its supporters. While proponents praised some of the steps the department took during Merrick Garland's tenure as Attorney General, such as the establishment of a database on corporate crime, the Biden DOJ also strongly relied on leniency agreements that allow companies to delay or avoid prosecution, and encourage them to scapegoat individual employees to avoid more serious charges. Kenneth Polite Jr., former Assistant Attorney General for the DOJ's Criminal Division, reviewed the corporate law compliance policy to limit prosecutions.
The debate over the government's closure is fueling a civil war within the Republican party in the chamber.

The most aggressive conservatives in the House of Representatives today blocked the party leadership, effectively halting a series of votes, in protest of the recent spending agreement reached by House Speaker Mike Johnson with Democratic leaders, which they deem inadequate regarding tax cuts.

While Louisiana Republicans may be able to avoid addressing this issue for now, the country will face a deadline on January 19th to pass four of the 12 annual spending bills. Johnson publicly stated that he would not support a "continuing resolution" (CR) to postpone the deadline for these four bills to the date of the other eight, which is February 2nd.

However, with this deadline just 9 days away, the leading Republican in the Senate, Mitch McConnell, stated that Congress will need to approve a continuing resolution to keep the government open, suggesting that the Speaker of the House may soon break a promise he made largely to appease conservatives. Such a move could trigger a heated ideological battle in a highly divided chamber over the role of the Republican Party in spending cuts, potentially leading to a partial government shutdown or Johnson's removal from office.

"I was very clear that CRs are not the way to fund our government, and that the 1974 budget law requires us to approve the 12 spending bills," said Montana Representative Matt Rosendale to Newsweek. "We had more than enough time to do so, and if the leaders don't instruct the committees to complete the work and allow members to vote on it, a shutdown will occur."

House Speaker Mike Johnson is photographed in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on December 12, 2023. Johnson is facing a rebellious Republican conference that is unable to reach an agreement on the level of government spending. Photograph by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images.

Rosendale, a member of the Freedom caucus on the right, was one of the individuals who blocked Wednesday's vote. He believes that the maximum figure in Johnson's agreement is too high and that it will not be sufficient to reduce the national debt of $34 trillion.

Rosendale is also among the 71 Republicans who oppose the Fiscal Responsibility Act, backed by Democrats and former President Kevin McCarthy; an agreement that could set the parameters for the recent negotiations between Johnson and the Democratic leader of the Senate, Charles Schumer.

Johnson celebrated the agreement to reduce spending by approximately $16 billion, but the Freedom Caucus believes that more could have been achieved. Moderate Republicans who supported McCarthy's agreement view this position as unrealistic and contrary to the Republican goal of forcing Congress to pass the 12 spending bills, rather than the "omnibus" measure from previous years, which combined those 12 bills into a single vote.

"It's a new year, but the same foolish behavior from some," said Republican representative for New York, Mike Lawler, to Newsweek. "We're not passing a large omnibus bill, so each proposed law will have to be debated and negotiated in a conference. Obviously, the reality is that we're likely going to need more time to do this. I don't support a government shutdown, so I don't see any problem with using a short-term continuing resolution to allow this process to be completed."

The Congress has not approved the 12 individual bills since 1996. Lawler stated that it is worth delaying the approval of four bills to ensure that the process is carried out correctly. If the Congress cannot approve the twelve bills by December, under the Budget Responsibility Act, a 1% cut in the military and civilian discretionary spending could be applied.

Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Republican and one of the most vocal and outspoken critics of the budget, but not one of those who protested on Wednesday, stated that an annual continuing resolution (CR) that triggers a 1% spending cut could be the most viable way to keep the government open while ending the current risky policy.

However, he assured that "the most responsible" way to cut spending would be to pass the 12 bills. Given that many Republicans are hesitant to support a government shutdown and a 1% reduction in military spending, the urgency to pass the bills could bring enough Republicans and Democrats together to extend the deadline for the four bills and reach an agreement to fund the government, even if it puts Johnson in a difficult position with those on the far right.

"The 1 percent cut is supposed to serve as a motivator, and we could use it to push through the 12 pieces of legislation," Massie told Newsweek. "Therefore, I believe we could implement a one-year plan, discuss it, and then we would encounter that small obstacle, which, hopefully, would motivate everyone to come to a consensus. That's how I would approach it."
Regulators approve new Bitcoin-backed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) at a crucial time for cryptocurrencies.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reluctantly approved exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that hold Bitcoin on Wednesday, a move that was highly anticipated by cryptocurrency enthusiasts and criticized by skeptical financial watchdogs within the cryptocurrency industry.
The commission approved 10 exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that invest in Bitcoin, including those proposed by major companies like Blackrock and Fidelity, as well as smaller financial firms.

“While we have approved the listing and trading of certain Bitcoin-related products, we have not approved or endorsed Bitcoin itself,” stated Gary Gensler, chairman of the SEC. “Investors should be cautious about the myriad of risks associated with Bitcoin and the products whose value is linked to cryptocurrencies.”
Gensler also added that the approval of Bitcoin funds does not mean that the SEC will automatically approve funds or exchange-traded products (ETPs) based on other currencies or digital assets.

According to Gensler, "today's action is significantly limited to ETPs that hold a product unrelated to security, such as Bitcoin. This should in no way imply that the Commission is willing to approve listing standards for crypto assets. This approval also says nothing about the Commission's perspective on the situation of other crypto assets according to federal laws, or on the current situation of non-compliance with federal securities laws by certain participants in the crypto asset market."

The SEC has rejected similar funding requests for years. However, last year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia ruled against the SEC's rejection of Grayscale's request to convert a derivative fund into one that would directly use bitcoins, effectively challenging the SEC's position.

“Based on this context and the circumstances discussed in more detail in the approval order, I believe the most sustainable path is to approve the listing and trading of these Bitcoin ETPs,” explained Gensler.

The highly anticipated approval was praised as a crucial step for digital currencies, which, according to its proponents, will make it easier to invest in Bitcoin and potentially lead to greater acceptance of cryptocurrencies as a legitimate financial asset. In recent months, the price of Bitcoin has surged, rising from approximately $25,000 in September to over $45,000, in part because many Bitcoin investors believe that ETFs will create greater demand for the asset.
Critics attacked the SEC on Wednesday evening.

Dennis M. Kelleher, co-founder, president, and CEO of Better Markets, stated that the approval is a "historic mistake" that will not only allow cryptocurrency predators to prey on tens of millions of investors and retirees, but will also weaken financial stability.

Keller added that "with the clearly anarchic cryptocurrency industry collapsing and burning due to countless arrests, criminal convictions, bankruptcies, lawsuits, scandals, massive losses, and millions of victims among investors and clients, who would have thought that the SEC would step in to rescue it by approving an investment vehicle that would allow the widespread sale of a financial product known for its uselessness, volatility, and for being completely fraudulent to the average American?"
Complaints about the use of the Russian language in Ukraine have increased by 30% (RT News, Russia and former Soviet Union)
Authorities are urging the public to report any information they have in an attempt to "de-radicalize" the country.

The number of complaints about people speaking Russian in Ukraine increased by 30% last year. Kiev is actively encouraging the population to report these cases, in what appears to be an attempt to protect the country from Russian influence.

According to the state's language protection commissioner's office, 3,692 violations of the language law were reported in 2023. Kiev, Kharkov, and Odessa were "the leaders in terms of the number of complaints and violations." Therefore, strict controls on the enforcement of citizens' linguistic rights in all areas of public life should be a priority for community leaders this year," stated the country's Language Defender, Taras Kremen.

Kremen also confirmed a fine of 3,400 hryvnias (USD 89) to a taxi driver in Kyiv for providing service to his clients in Russian. The Human Rights Commissioner reminded the public about the "detailed protocol of actions to be taken in cases of violation of the right to receive information or services in the state language," urging the public to immediately file complaints on the commissioner's website when such cases occur.

In 2019, Ukraine passed a law requiring the use of Ukrainian in all areas of public life, including government, medicine, education, and media. Non-compliance can result in penalties. Since 2022, when the conflict with Russia began, Ukraine has launched a "de-Russification" campaign, with lawmakers arguing that it is necessary to counter Russian influence. Local authorities have imposed a complete ban on Russian-language art, performances, books, films, and songs, as well as their study in schools and universities, and have recommended that schoolchildren communicate in Ukrainian, even during breaks.

In August, a teenage singer was briefly arrested and forced to record a video of an apology after performing songs by the Soviet singer Viktor Tsoy in the city of Lviv. The dismissal of several teachers who spoke Russian to their students also sparked public protests.

The Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine, Alexey Danilov, had previously stated that "the Russian language must disappear" from Ukrainian territory "because it is an element of hostile propaganda and brainwashing for the population."

Moscow argues that such laws violate the rights of the Russian-speaking population, which includes approximately half of the inhabitants of Ukraine. Russian Foreign Minister Maria Zakharova stated in February that Kyiv's "discriminatory campaign" against the Russian language was becoming increasingly "unacceptable." A survey conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that discrimination against the Russian language was the most common prejudice in Ukraine, with 45% of respondents citing it as a problem.
Let's not allow the Scottish National Party (SNP) to turn the healthcare crisis into "the new normal" (as reported in The Scotsman).
As the latest figures from the National Health Service (NHS) reveal more concerning news, we should be outraged.

An 83-hour wait in the emergency room, with four out of ten patients waiting for more than four hours, 30 ambulances queuing outside a hospital, an inability to answer other emergency calls, and staff "finishing their shifts in tears" due to the level of care, and a "nearly complete collapse of service delivery," according to an expert from the Royal College of Emergency Medicine.

If anyone dares to say that the NHS in Scotland is not in crisis, or that this is simply due to typical winter problems, we should be outraged. The danger lies in politicians like the beleaguered Health Secretary, Michael Matheson, succeeding in convincing us that, while regrettable, this is somehow acceptable, and that ministers have little they can do in these circumstances, that this is the new normal.

Despite calls for resignations due to the SNP's failure to implement the NSH recovery plan, Matheson stated that "the harsh winter" is "not exclusive to Scotland." Instead of blaming Westminster, the attempt to defend the situation was to argue that "Westminster is equally deficient," as if this would offer some comfort to the legions of patients forced to wait for endless hours, suffering pain and distress.

He acknowledged that the long-standing problem of delayed discharges, where patients who are medically fit to leave the hospital are unable to do so, often due to a lack of necessary social support, was a "key factor," but assured that a plan of action was being "implemented effectively." Given that this has been a persistent issue for years, few people have high expectations that the new strategy will finally find a solution.

In fact, figures from Public Health Scotland show that the situation is actually worsening: 1,910 people experienced delays in hospitals in November, and as many as 1,730 in April. One of the reasons why ambulances cannot quickly transfer patients is that emergency services are overwhelmed because the waiting rooms are full.

Based on the current state of our hospitals, the SNP's speech about recovery plans and action plans is simply that: a speech, and furthermore, a dangerous one. We must not allow incompetent politicians to make us complicit in the disappearance of the great British institution that is the National Health Service.
A construction waste recycling company is opening a new plant in Cumbernauld as part of the circular economy initiative.
This expansion will also help to transform the abandoned Gartshore Works site.
A Scottish recycling company, which had already processed over a million tons of construction waste, opened a second plant following a multi-million dollar investment.

Brewster Brothers' recycling plants transform 100% of the excavated earth and construction debris they process into high-value aggregates for reuse. Over the past six years, the facilities located near Livingston (West Lothian) have prevented the disposal of 1.35 million tons of construction, demolition, and excavation waste. They have created over one million tons of recycled aggregates for sale to the industry.

As part of a business expansion exceeding £6 million, Brewster has now opened its second facility, revitalizing the former Gartshore Works near Cumbernauld. The new facility will serve construction sites and residential and public service developments in the Central Belt. The facility, located near Livingston and currently employing 39 people, will continue to provide sustainable and recycled aggregate services to businesses in Edinburgh, Fife, and the Lothians.

The CEO, Scott Brewster, who started this business with his father in 2017, Alex, stated: “It is becoming increasingly clear that the construction sector in Scotland recognizes the need to reduce the amount of natural resources used by the industry, as well as the amount of coal it emits, while simultaneously increasing the use of recycled and secondary materials. The volume of construction and excavation waste that has been recycled over the past six years has grown enormously, and our investment in these secondary facilities demonstrates that there is still significant potential for further expansion in this area.”

"Scotland has a strong ambition to transition towards a circular economy, and the government plans to introduce a new tax on aggregates, which should accelerate the shift towards the use of virgin materials."

As part of the redevelopment of the abandoned Gartshore Works facilities, the company recruited new employees, supported by the Scottish Enterprise Green Jobs Fund. The company will also recycle the former mine waste landfill, and the area will be transformed into a rural park for the local community.
Politicians make mistakes when it comes to setting rent limits.

Politicians are always tempted to intervene in situations where they believe they can make a difference. Logically, if there were a simple and obvious solution to a problem, someone with more knowledge and understanding in that area would have already implemented it.

Therefore, the "Cost of Living (Tenant Protection) Act 2022" was introduced in Scotland almost 18 months ago, with the aim of limiting rental prices for a period of time to alleviate the pressures of the cost of living crisis. However, the latest surveys by the Scottish government now reveal that, in the last year alone, the average rental prices of all types of properties, regardless of size, have increased from 11.7 percent for one-bedroom properties to the highest figure of 14.3 percent for two-bedroom homes. All types of properties, from four-bedroom homes to one-bedroom homes, have seen double-digit increases in their rental prices since the Cost of Living Act was introduced in October 2022, tripling the average annual rental increases of the previous 12 years.

Everyone involved in the housing sector had warned that this would happen, but their concerns were ignored. The failure to recognize that market forces, rather than the government, dictate prices led to the significant increase in rental costs, which could have been avoided with greater knowledge, negotiation, and discussion with this sector, as well as a plan that understood the principles of supply and demand.

With the passage of the Cost of Living Law on March 31, 2024, a new consultation aims to expand the limits on rent increases that could be applied next year. The consultation concludes this Monday and proposes setting rent prices based on the lowest of three comparisons: the market rental price, a proposed new rental price from the landlord, and a "reasonable" increase based on a new progressive reduction system, comparing a percentage of the market rental price.
Scottish tenants are likely to face alarming rent increases if they don't seek expert advice (Photo: Adobe)

This proposed gradual reduction would set rent increases between 6 percent and a maximum of 15 percent, which, ironically, would represent an increase compared to the historical annual rate of price increases. However, even more importantly, this system would be difficult to manage, excessively complex, and prohibitively expensive to monitor and implement. We already have a system in place where the initial court controls whether a rent is fair. This would simply add more layers of bureaucracy without any benefit for landlords or tenants.

Unfortunately, this consultation appears to be a new attempt to impose controls on the sector. A much simpler solution would be to return the market to its normal state and avoid imposing external controls on rental prices, which would result in more moderate increases than we have seen in the last 18 months. To stabilize rental prices in the long term, the government should encourage greater investment and growth in the private rental sector (PRS), while simultaneously funding significant growth in social housing. Greater investment in the PRS will lead to greater stability in the housing sector. Increasing volumes in both the PRS and social housing markets will achieve stability over time, as demand will match supply and a balance will be reached. Only by implementing these measures will we begin to address the current housing crisis. Anything else simply won't work.
Greggs plans to increase its profits through greater expansion of its stores, while maintaining its prices.
The company, which is listed on the FTSE 250 and is known for its sausage rolls and oven-baked steaks, plans to expand its network of stores, but not its prices.
Greggs, the bakery chain, has stated that it does not plan to raise prices next year and that it aims to open 160 new stores, while seeking locations outside of city centers.

Roisin Currie, the CEO, told PA that "she currently has no plans to increase prices" and expects a more stable cost base in the coming year. However, she added that "it could be a long time before we experience deflation" which would allow the group to start reducing prices. She noted that retailers are among those facing higher wage costs due to the minimum wage increase. Nevertheless, she added that this upward trend in wages also represents "good news, as it puts more money in consumers' pockets."

Greggs also announced its plans to open another 160 stores next year and celebrated a strong end to 2023. The group set a record by opening 220 new stores in 2023, with 33 closures and 42 relocations, resulting in a net total of 145 new locations, bringing the total to 2,473 properties.

The FTSE 250 company plans to open between 140 and 160 net sales points in 2024, with the aim of making it easier for its customers to access its stores. It will continue to try to expand in shopping centers, tourist areas, roadside locations, and industrial estates. "Wherever there is a location where it is currently difficult to access a Greggs, that is where we want to try to establish ourselves," said Currie.

The company also plans to extend evening hours selectively, with an extension already available in 1,200 of its stores. In a recent business update, the company reported a 9.4 percent increase in comparable sales from its company-owned stores during the last quarter, a deceleration of 14.2 percent from the growth experienced in the previous three months, as Greggs noted that the impact of rising prices was less significant. The year-on-year comparable growth reached 13.7 percent, with a total annual sales increase of a fifth, valued at £1.8 billion.

The company also stated that it continues to see increased demand for vegan options, and therefore, it is once again offering its vegan steak, as well as its festive range, which includes the holiday cake, chocolate and orange muffin, and the festive baguette lunch.

Matt Britzman, a purchasing and sales analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, stated that Greggs "could consider 2023 as a year of real progress" thanks to its extended opening hours, increased delivery options, improved supply chain, and "a new range of tasty snacks." She added: "Christmas cakes and chocolate and orange muffins are leading the way, but the overall market points to a decline in sales throughout the year, with the fourth quarter being the lowest of 2023. This is primarily because Greggs was able to limit price increases as inflation slowed. In the long term, this is a positive development."

"One of Greggs' main strengths is offering affordable treats, and maintaining this approach is crucial, especially when consumers have limited incomes. Politicians who believe they can overrule court decisions are, in effect, placing themselves above the law.

As The Scotsman and others have pointed out for years, the unjust conviction of hundreds of post office branch managers in the Horizon scandal is one of the greatest failures of the justice system in history. People were sent to prison, marriages and reputations were destroyed, homes were lost, and many innocent individuals were treated as criminals.

The first concern is that a general law that exonerates hundreds of people could unintentionally include some who are guilty, but, given the urgent need to acquit the innocent, it could be a price worth paying. The second concern is more alarming: a law that overturns court verdicts could set a dangerous precedent at a time when populist movements are testing the limits of political power.

In the United Kingdom, Boris Johnson illegally suspended Parliament to advance his Brexit plans, while Sunak aims to overturn the Supreme Court's decision that Rwanda is not a safe country by passing a law stating otherwise.

The concept of separation of powers (the government, the parliament, and the judicial branch) is a vital safeguard against tyranny. Let's restore oversight of Washington's prisons: lives depend on it.

The Washington state prison system is facing a mortality crisis. This is an uncomfortable but unavoidable reality that we, as co-presidents of a legislative working group tasked with studying the state's prison system and recommending changes to make prisons safer, are confronting. Although we come from different backgrounds, such as prison administration, civil rights advocacy, and personal experience with incarceration, we all agree that there should be independent oversight of Washington's prisons.

More than 130,000 people were incarcerated in a Washington state prison in 2022, yet there is a surprising lack of information about what happens once they arrive there. Washington state lacks a state office to oversee prisons and provide data to the public. Some of the only available data refers to deaths while in custody.

What we have discovered demonstrates that immediate action is necessary. Even considering the increase in the Washington population, the death rate in its prisons nearly tripled between 2000 and 2019 (an increase 16 times greater than the national average). Washington currently has the fourth highest prison mortality rate in the nation. This cannot continue.

Reversing the trend of mortality in prisons, and addressing the many other problems our prisons face, may require difficult political decisions. However, independent oversight of prisons is a crucial first step towards a safer and more humane prison system. Independent oversight has proven to be an effective method for improving transparency and accountability, both in Washington and throughout the rest of the country. According to our estimates, at least 25 states have a state office responsible for overseeing prisons, and all of them have a lower mortality rate than Washington.

In our case, Washington has recently established or expanded independent oversight in prisons, police departments, schools, and other state entities. Prisons are a notable exception to this oversight among institutions responsible for the health and safety of tens of thousands of people.

An independent oversight office for prisons can monitor their condition, hold meetings with staff and inmates, report on situations they have personally witnessed, and even raise concerns before any injuries occur. A prison oversight office can also collect data and provide information, helping administrators, legislators, and the public to understand our prison system and promote solutions, based on this data, to reduce mortality rates in prisons and other related problems.

Supervision is not only focused on the benefit of the incarcerated. Our working group has identified that a supervision office can collaborate with overwhelmed prison systems to facilitate necessary assistance and recommendations, including smart policies to promote employee safety and reduce recidivism.

The state of Washington had a state-level prison oversight office from 1981 to 1987, which was once praised by the U.S. Department of Justice as a model for the country's prison systems. Unfortunately, the legislature eliminated the state's prison oversight, despite objections from prison administrators and civil rights groups, among others.

Independent oversight would foster public trust and data-driven decision-making in an area that has long operated outside of transparency. We are calling on the legislative branch to enact our working group's recommendation to restore independent oversight of municipal, regional, and state prisons. The lives of people depend on it.
Hailey Ockinga is an advocate against incarceration and a community organizer, as well as the executive director of Beyond These Walls, in the state of Washington.
Ethan Frenchman is a lawyer at Disability Rights Washington, where he represents individuals with disabilities in prisons and jails.
How to tell if you're flying on a Boeing 737 MAX

For most travelers, the type of aircraft is not a deciding factor when booking a flight. However, with the majority of Boeing 737 MAX 9 aircraft grounded across the country following the Alaska Airlines incident on January 6th, some potential passengers may want to know what type of aircraft they will be using and which models are considered the safest. The first question is relatively straightforward; the second is a bit more complex.

The type of aircraft is usually specified in the flight booking information. In Google Flights, it is included in the flight details when a listing is expanded, and it is typically listed on the individual airline pages. If, for any reason, the aircraft type does not appear in Google Flights or on the booking page, websites like Expert Flyer and SeatGuru collect flight information, including seat maps and aircraft type.

Determining the safest aircraft models is not straightforward. The National Transportation Safety Board possesses comprehensive databases with information on accidents and incidents. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) also provides preliminary reports on accidents and incidents over the past 10 days, including the manufacturer of the involved aircraft, on its Aviation Safety Information and Exchange website.

The FAA also provides a link to another useful resource: Boeing's World Statistical Summary of Jet Aircraft Accidents from 1959 to 2022, which evaluates safety based on aircraft type, with an accident breakdown by model. According to the report, published in September 2023, the Boeing 787 and the Airbus A350 are the aircraft models with the fewest total hull losses, which are accidents in which the aircraft is completely destroyed and cannot be repaired. There are a few other models in the report that never experienced a hull loss, such as the two-deck Airbus A380, but those models had accumulated fewer than 1 million take-offs at the time the report was published.

The report also includes a comparison of hull loss rates per million take-offs, taking into account that some models are more common or have been in service for longer than others. The Airbus A310, introduced in 1983, has the highest hull loss rate, at 2.53 per million take-offs, among the models still in service as passenger aircraft. The Airbus 320 family, including the A321 and A319neo, has the lowest rate, at 0.11. The Boeing 737 MAX, which has been in service since 2017, has an accumulated rate of 1.48.

It is important to note that, although these figures are per million flights, some of the aircraft models mentioned in the report, such as the Boeing 727 presented in 1964, have been in operation for decades, and therefore have had more time to accumulate accidents than other models.

Perry Cooper, a media representative for the Port of Seattle, who oversees the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, stated in an email that there are a wide range of factors that contribute to accidents, ranging from equipment malfunctions to human error. Therefore, while it is relatively straightforward to determine the type of aircraft you will be flying on, it is more complex to understand what that means from a safety perspective.

While you can compare aircraft models based on the available information, the FAA recommends avoiding comparing airlines based on their accident reports. According to a report cited by the administration, "there is currently no evidence in the accident data to allow for the classification of individual airlines based on their safety records."

According to the FAA, while there are significant differences in airline safety records at specific times, this is primarily due to the "infrequent but catastrophic nature of an aviation accident," and these apparent differences between airlines tend to even out over time. The FAA declined our request for comment.
How Betta Edu became the scapegoat for a dysfunctional political system

Furthermore, it goes on to say that "any public official who deposits public funds into a private account will be considered to be doing so for fraudulent purposes."

Celeste is my favorite example of a "small, good freeware game that eventually became a massive, commercially successful game with completely over-the-top graphics." In the original version, the double-speed ability is a powerful boost that is obtained from a treasure chest, but in the commercial version, it makes me want to cry.

Overall, I really enjoy the interaction between the two types of stories. The advantage of short stories is that you can "jump right into the good part": they immediately grab your attention and make you feel good. The advantage of longer stories is that you can build up more emotional intensity, sacrificing immediacy for a more intense result.

The climax of Celeste, the commercial game, is essentially a much larger version of the original PICO-8 game, with several hours of gameplay that make it stand out even more. Celeste is proud of the original game, which includes references like the memorial monument, the "2,000 meters, 2,500 meters..." progression, the power-up, and the flag at the top. It even lets you play the original game from the main menu!

Celeste is not "the improved version" or "the final version" of the PICO-8 game; rather, it's a different approach to the same core story. As someone who enjoys both the short and long versions, seeing this connection laid out in this way is truly interesting and wonderful.

There's another intermediate version that could have existed between the two, which tells the same story in a more detailed and well-developed way, but with a more appropriate length and less outlandish production values. I believe that would have been my favorite version – a more emotionally resonant… well, as it stands now, the main arc for those who play the game is essentially just a small part of it; they're more interested in creating a great platforming experience than anything else. Nevertheless, I think it's great.

My mind was racing with confused thoughts, and many of them were filled with anger, but also with sadness. I had done a lot of research on the outer cities and the infected capital, Alcatraz, which they had named after the prison. It seemed to fit the name quite well, as I had read. And, of course, the uninfected had cut off all remaining connections to the infected territory. It was… tragic.

The journey home was peaceful, but incredibly noisy. Disturbing thoughts plagued my mind, and the regret of not staying to help filled me with anxiety several times. Finally, I arrived home, almost in tears from the terrifying walk amidst the deafening sounds of thunder coming from the clouds above me. Sometimes, the loud noises were enough to scare anyone. Dad was already asleep on the sofa, watching a rerun of an old movie, probably from 10 or 12 years ago. Sighing, I quietly returned to my room. She couldn't say the same for Thassalin, who lay motionless, slumped against the only tree that hadn't collapsed under her weight. Nyssi did everything she could to reach Thassalin, but she could barely see more than a few meters ahead. Everything was completely dark and shrouded in ominous shadows. And within those shadows, something was groaning and creaking.

Nyssi shrugged and then, using her camera, took some pictures of the creatures, which were now definitely dead. As the guards escorted her to that point, the people shouted in outrage at the sight of their only queen, and the kindest of them, about to be killed. Some were crying, others were shouting and trying to attack the guards, while others were wondering why this was happening, but they all shared the same feeling.
"Let her go!"
"Why are they doing this to him?"

As Eirwen approached the wooden post, the most feared person in the kingdom appeared: the man of fire. The former queen, Eirwen, was about to die in the flames. No one deserved such a death, not even the criminals. It was the most cruel thing that could be done to a person in Frostfell.

Eirwen was tied to the wooden post, and the king began to speak about how the queen had betrayed them all. The people of Frostfell refused to believe him, never accepting his words. It was then that the man with fire set the post ablaze, and a single tear rolled down the face of the former queen.
"Live, Kari." That was the end of Queen Eirwen's reign.
Silence in the halls

Tap, tap, tap. That was all you could hear from the furthest room on the left side of the southern wing of the palace, a room that was perpetually cold. The servants who passed by there always wondered what was in the room, and were actually afraid of what they might find. The maids spread rumors throughout the halls. It was believed that the late Queen of Ice, Eirwen, was in that room, waiting to be released.
"They couldn't be more wrong," Ivory thought, walking towards the southern wing, as the maids bustled around, whispering to each other. They have absolutely no idea what's inside.
Of course, the rumors also applied to her, as she was the only person allowed to enter the room.
"Knock, knock. 'Lady Kari, are you there?'" Ivory whispered against the elaborate door, decorated with snowflakes and a crown, the symbol of the royal family.

He wondered if she would actually let him in, unlike the previous times he had tried to ask. "I still have a bruise from the last time," Ivory said with a smile. Kari had thrown a book at his shoulder, but when she saw who it was, she immediately apologized.
There was a single, forceful blow from the inside, as if to say, "I was here." Ultimately, there was nowhere else to go.
"Can I come in?", Ivory asked, recalling the time he had entered without asking first.

An attack from within. That's what it seemed to be saying. Ivory shivered, both from the cold and from the sound. It seemed strange to hear a noise coming from a room that was supposedly empty, even though he had been entering it for years.

"I'm coming in now," Ivory said, slowly opening the door. What he saw inside was unusual, even for someone who wasn't considered "normal." There were papers everywhere, books scattered around, the desk was broken, and there were multiple ice sculptures also strewn about. Without any windows, the light was dim, if not nonexistent. It was also colder than the rest of the palace (which was already quite cold). The room seemed as if it had been ravaged by a snowstorm.
The young woman in the room was curled up in bed, wrapped in a duvet while reading one of the notebooks. A small lamp illuminated the space.
"What's that notebook?", Ivory asked, sitting down next to Kari on her bed.
They turned the page to a blank one and wrote the date. Below that, they wrote: "11/5/648 - 13/12/648".
"Looking over old memories?", Ivory asked, looking at the old notebook. Kari nodded. "Do you think they'll let you out for Christmas? There are only a few days left."

Kari managed to get two hits in the game. No, not as Ivory predicted. King Ice never allowed Kari to play, as he considered her "a liability." She was born mute and was the only girl in her family, which consisted entirely of men.

Ivory was also like that, in her own way. When Ivory came out as non-binary, it felt like the world had changed too. She was offered jobs that required her to be isolated for most of the time, as a form of punishment for being different.
I also had to work as a lady-in-waiting to the princess. Ivory didn't mind this at all, as it also allowed them to form a friendship.
"Your birthday is coming up soon, isn't it?" Ivory asked, remembering that the princess's birthday was just a few days away. Kari nodded, with a sad look in her blue eyes.
"Do you want to celebrate it?" he asked, thinking about the last time she had answered.

"No," Kari replied, with a dismissive wave of her hand. "Ivory knew this was a delicate matter for her. It was the day she was confined to her room and her mother was banished. Ivory was just a baby at the time, but she remembered the anger that had gripped the servants and the people of the village. She had heard that Queen Eirwen was a good queen, but also that she strangely predicted events that later came to pass.
"So… what do you want to do?", he asked. Kari looked up, her face filled with excitement. She handed Ivory a piece of paper. But when he read it…
15 cm x 15 cm painting canvas.
White paint, various shades of blue.
Six different sizes of brushes.
Tripod.

"Would you like me to bring these things for you?", Ivory asked, turning to the quiet princess, who was tapping her fingers nervously while her pigtails swung back and forth. "Yes?" She let out a small laugh, noticing that the princess, who was usually reserved, was excited about something. It was the first time she had asked for something that wasn't related to books and that wasn't within her room.
"Great! Shall we meet later?", Ivory asked, standing up and navigating through the pile of papers and notebooks.
Kari nodded, returning to her memories and snuggling into her thick blanket.
He left the room, feeling relieved that the princess had finally stepped outside of her comfort zone and requested things beyond her reach, such as art supplies.
He walked through the halls again, trying once more to ignore the whispers of the maids.
"I've heard that she's being possessed by the Queen Eirwen, which is why she always goes to that room."
"I've heard that it eats children in that room."
"She looks like a man, and that's not a bad thing."
He covered his ears, as simply ignoring the whispers wasn't working. He headed to the real painter's room, which was located on the east wing, the second door on the left.

Ivory approached the door, which was just as intricate as Kari's. It depicted the White Dragon, one of the six primordial dragons supposedly responsible for creating Frostfell. It made sense for the painter to have this dragon on his door; he enjoyed the story.

She opened the door, expecting to see the usual mess: paint splatters everywhere, pencils and papers scattered around the room, easels covering every inch of the wall. To her surprise, she found something completely different. The room was spotless, with a red velvet backdrop and a stool in front. On the stool sat the heir, posing for a portrait.
“Ah, good morning, Ivory! Would you like to see your future king getting his portrait taken?” he asked, winking.
"I'm sorry, little prince," he said, partly ignoring him while searching for the things his quiet friend wanted. "I'm only here to find some artistic supplies."
"Oh, the little one is leaving so soon?" asked Aquilo, "But I was really looking forward to seeing you!"
"Well, I'm not." Ivory found the items on her list and placed them in a drawer nearby. "And I'm not a girl."
But the prince didn't think that way. "Oh, darling, you know it's just an expression! It will pass when you're older," he said, dragging out the words.

"I need to leave," he said, suddenly feeling uncomfortable in the face of the prince's response. He remembered all the negative things people had said about his gender identity. "I really want to distance myself from him," he thought.
"Are you leaving so soon?" The prince appeared at the door like a flash, ignoring the shouts of a certain royal painter.
"That's not how a future king should behave!" he exclaimed.

"No hay forma de que nadie se entere. People won't believe you, and the painter won't say anything if he values his life." He glanced back at the painter for a second, then leaned further towards Ivory. "What do you say to going out together?" He shuddered. Obviously, he had heard multiple threats in the past, but never from a prince, and certainly not from the next in line to become king.
"Do you even know what the word 'no' means?" he exclaimed, pushing the heir to the throne a considerable distance away.
"No," replied the entity, with a smile. Of course, the heir to the throne, who gets everything he wants, has no idea what that word means.
Ivory looked up. "Why do you want to go out with me, compared to everyone else? I mean, I don't know, there must be at least 100 other people interested in dating me."
He interrupted her, still smiling, "Actually, it's 500." He pushed his hair back, waving it in the cold air.
"See? You're asking 'why'? I'm a walking threat." He gently squeezed his arms.
"You're the most beautiful girl I've ever seen." He placed a finger under Ivory's chin, forcing her to look at him.
Chapter 1
Cohren

04:30 Itania time. Cohren hated waking up this early. Basically, because it was his responsibility to wake up the rest of his unit. He quietly got out of his bunk to put on his combat uniform; he put on his assault vest and grabbed his belongings from his locker, being careful with a small box in particular. He slung his rifle over his shoulder and put on his helmet, which was attached to a small hook on his belt. He had everything he needed: respirator, goggles, and all the other essentials. After checking the ammunition in his pouches, he quietly left the barracks, the mud and ice crunching under the soles of his boots.

He pulled a lighter from his jacket pocket and a cigarette from the other. As he lit it, he took a drag before opening the door a little. In the past week, he had had to be resourceful when waking up the men and women under his command. He had stopped using the default alarm, which only worked about half the time, and the only sound coming from the speakers was a faint whistle.
"It's time to wake them up." Cohren turned to see the second lieutenant Nemic approaching.
"Yes," Cohren replied.
"What are you planning to use this time?"
Before I could respond, the door opened and Harris, Craith, and a few others quickly emerged, already fully dressed and equipped.
"Good morning," Craith said.
"What woke them up, guys?" Cohren asked.

"Well, first of all, we didn't want to find out what they were planning to do to wake up the company today. Second, the first units to get up are the ones who get to choose breakfast," said one of the men, Ravik. "And you know how they take it."
"He's absolutely right, expert," Cohren said. He reached into his pocket and pressed a switch. A loud, piercing alarm began to sound inside the barracks. He heard muffled shouts and people stumbling.
"Valturi, honestly," Nemic said. "You'd think by now they would have learned to wake up when I do."

"Well, these guys here at the training camp definitely learned that." Cohren gestured towards Harris, Craith, and Ravik. "But of course, they are squad and platoon leaders, and they know they need to get up before their units."

Moments later, the rest of the company followed in a rush. Everyone had what they needed, from personal items to the necessary equipment. Some of the newest recruits seemed disoriented, while others appeared more annoyed.
"Good morning, everyone," Cohren said with a cheerful tone.
"With all due respect, Sergeant, why do you have to wake us up like this?" asked a member of the Shock Troops.
"Because regular alarms are useless. And because Alborada doesn't stay in bed," Cohren said.

"Make sure you have all your personal belongings with you," Cohren continued. As first lieutenant and first officer, it was his responsibility to oversee and assist the company, along with the company commander, Captain Boradin Shaw. "We are not returning. Sergeants and lieutenants, I am giving you and your squads fifteen minutes to conduct final checks and load up on today's rations."

The members of the Éxodo company quickly dispersed. They were part of the 2nd assault division of the 2nd army. They began as two separate companies, Cohorte and Daga, before merging. They were a company with internal divisions, and Cohren had mixed feelings about being promoted to first lieutenant, mainly due to this.

Cohren and Nemic, the leader of the first platoon, walked together under the light of the many lights at the forward operating base, which were powered by generators. Most of the lights were painted red to help conceal them from enemy bombers. Albor had used suppression attacks against the defenses, both in the air and on the ground, to combat them.
"Another day, another job for those of us heading straight to hell," Nemic said, with a sarcastic tone. "Where are we being sent this time?"

"To a base like this, on the outskirts of Ianlos. They send us in to assist with the ground assault," Cohren replied, taking a drag from his cigarette. Part of him blamed Craith for introducing him to smoking, but a year of combat takes its toll, so he didn't say anything.

"Damn. Things are getting really bad here," Nemic muttered. "All the news coming out of here is along the lines of 'Support the war effort. Send aid to the Kurgan front,' but what about sending aid to the Howland front?"

"Amen, brother," Cohren said, gesturing with his fingers to flick the cigarette ashes into the mud. "Anyway, we're moving with the first armored platoon, so we don't have to walk. Captain Shaw should be there already."
"Did Shaw arrange transportation for us?" Nemic asked, a little surprised.
"Well, yes. Actually, it's not as bad as I initially thought. I mean, it's not amazing, but it's also not unbearable."

Cohren raised his thumb and index finger to his throat microphone, adjusting the backpack on his back as he did so. “To all units of Company Exodus: meet at the west vehicle park when you are finished. We will depart with the first armored platoon at 05:00.”

Every few seconds, I would receive a response from the squad leaders. Harris, Craith, and Ravik were non-commissioned officers when they arrived. The four had been close friends since basic training on Earth. It seemed like a very long time had passed since I last saw Cohren, even though it had only been about two years. They were squad leaders, but Craith was now in charge of the 2nd platoon, having taken over a week ago after the previous leader was medically discharged following an injury from a sniper attack by the "Dawn" group.

As they made their way towards the vehicle depot, Cohren and Nemic worked on a group of approximately eight Kronos combat tanks and four Strykers. Their teams bustled around, ensuring that the vehicles were ready for deployment. Cohren's gaze soon fell upon Captain Boradin Shaw, who was speaking with the commander of the armored platoon. As they approached, Shaw looked at them and approached with his usual impassive expression, concealing any emotion.
"Sergeant Nemic… Sergeant Valturi…" he said slowly, looking at Cohren's pistol holster before looking up again. "I suppose the company is ready."

"Yes, Lieutenant. They should be on their way; we've given them time to get rations from the mess hall." At precisely 5:00 AM, the Exodus company gathered at the vehicle park. Shaw climbed onto a platform and began to speak.

"We are relocating to FOB I-131, which is 80 kilometers from Ianlos. We will be providing support for the ongoing siege and subsequent assault on Ianlos to eliminate the insurgency. From there, we will have a secure position at the base of the mountains," Shaw explained. "Go with your squads and ride."

The group dispersed, each with their own squad, while the sergeants directed them onto their respective tanks. Cohren climbed into one at the head of the convoy, joining Nemic, Craith, and two new recruits. Cohren remembered that they had arrived a few days ago, but he didn't know much about them. Sitting to the side, with his legs dangling, he adjusted his backpack and radio, which was connected to his headset and throat microphone.
"Hey, Cohren, does Harris still have Snowball?", Nemic asked as they settled in.
"Are you referring to the chicken that was stolen?" Cohren recalled the morning when it was stolen from a farm. "Yes, I think so."
Cohren glanced at one of the other tanks and saw Harris with his squad. In the back of his backpack, he could just make out the movement of a chick, its head bobbing as it surveyed the surroundings.
"Yes, we still have it," Cohren replied, as the hatch on the tank turret swung open with a metallic clang, revealing his commander.

"All the moving tanks," the commander said calmly but clearly into his headset. The engines of one of the tank platoons and the Strykers roared to life and began to move forward. The Kronos of Cohren released the brakes and continued, forming up. The tanks advanced in a wedge formation as they moved across the plains of Itania. The winter storms had frozen the marshes and forests, but the mud was always there.
After about an hour, one of the new recruits, whom Cohren recalled was named Orson, asked: "Sir, you've been with us since the start of the war, haven't you?"
"Yes, since Operation Firestorm," Cohren replied. "We thought it would be over in a few weeks, but… we underestimated it."

"Underestimating them is an understatement," Nemic added. "They had more weapons and personnel than we anticipated. They were able to take down the UFS Revenant in the first two weeks, and just last month, the Erebus. Honestly, we should be observing them from this route we're taking."
"Well, I will defend the Federation with courage," Orson said defiantly. "I won't let those terrorists intimidate me."
"You might say that now, but from what I've seen, most young recruits your age run for cover the moment they hear a gunshot," Craith retorted.
"I suppose we'll figure it out eventually," Cohren said, laughing. Orson didn't continue the conversation.
"First Officer Exodus, Commander Exodus." The Cohren radio crackled. "We are detecting thermal signatures at 320 meters, 20 degrees to the right."
Cohren climbed to the top of the tank and put on his optical goggles. When switching to thermal mode, he was able to see the signatures in the distance.
"Yes, I can see them," Cohren replied, using his throat microphone.
"Are they enemies?" asked the other recruit, Natayla.
"I don't know," Cohren said. He reached for the microphone and spoke: "Exodus Company, do not open fire unless we are fired upon. We're going to get them out of there."

As they approached, the small thermal signatures transitioned from indistinct spots to more defined shapes. One of them moved towards something and grasped it before quickly returning to the small ridge they were on. The figures positioned themselves for aiming.

"Contact!", Shaw shouted over the radio as they were being targeted by orange-colored machine guns from the ridge. Bullets struck the sides of the tanks as the assault troops jumped from the vehicles and took cover behind them. A tank-killing missile whizzed past, shaking their heads, before crashing to the ground behind the formation, exploding and sending debris onto one of the tanks. Another hit the side of a Stryker, and exploded. The crew scrambled for cover as the ammunition began to detonate.

"Iron 1-2 and 1-3, 25 degrees to the right, 275 meters! Open fire!" the tank platoon commander shouted over the radio. Iron 1-2 and 1-3 opened fire. Their projectiles struck the ridge and exploded, sending mud and rocks flying through the air.

"Send in the Centis!" shouted Knoxx, who was watching the ridge through binoculars. The back of one of the Cerberus opened, and a disarmed soldier climbed out, carrying special headphones. He shouted orders into a square microphone, and two Centis, formally known as Sentinels, rushed out. Their thin, metallic arms and legs swung forward, and they began to run. They were armed, but with their weapons hanging at their backs.
"Kill or capture?" Craith asked, as they watched.

"It looks like we've got him," Cohren speculated as the two sentinels vanished into the cloud of ash and smoke. Shouts and gunfire echoed from the ridge, but quickly ceased. A moment later, the two sentinels reappeared, dragging someone behind them. When they returned to the safety of the ranks, they threw the figure to the ground, who groaned in pain as it slammed against the mud and snow.
Shaw approached the figure, which was beginning to stand up. Then, he turned to one of the guards: "How many?"
"Three dead, my lieutenant," the sentry replied. "The rest fled on foot."
Shaw nodded and turned to Cohren and Criath, who were standing nearby. "Would you be so kind as to ensure this man is kept safe?"
